correctness.rationale: For both scalar fields the polynomial norm equals the spectral norm of its symmetric coefficient matrix. Orthogonal diagonalization/Takagi factorization decomposes each symmetric contraction as a convex combination of symmetric orthogonal/unitary matrices. The exact coefficient identity E=2||A||_F²−sum|A_ii|² therefore reduces the optimum to minimizing squared diagonal magnitude over such unitaries. In real odd dimension the integral odd trace and Cauchy give δ≥1/n, met by a constant-diagonal Fourier projection reflection; even real dimension has zero-diagonal transposition blocks. In complex dimension three the unitary diagonal cofactor identities imply (3−δ)/2≤√(3δ)+δ and hence δ≥1/3, attained by a 3×3 Householder reflection. An explicitly defined symmetric zero-diagonal 5×5 Fourier multiplier unitary, plus transposition blocks, handles odd complex n≥5. All equality constructions have operator norm exactly one; n=1 is checked separately. A direct numerical check in dimensions 1--9 supplemented, but was not used as a proof, including no extrapolation beyond tested n.

value.rationale: This is a complete natural finite-dimensional classification of the sharp global coefficient ℓ2 constant for quadratic polynomials at the Hilbert critical endpoint, not a recomputation of the asymptotic exponent. It distinguishes odd real dimensions, identifies a genuine 3×3 complex cofactor obstruction and constructs complex zero-diagonal symmetric unitaries at the first feasible odd dimension five. The scalar-field split and explicit extremizers resolve the natural question of when the universal √(2n) bound is attainable; the field- and dimension-specific answers are not implied by the known exponent alone. There is plausible utility whenever sharp constants, finite-coordinate cutoff estimates, and equality cases matter in polynomial Hardy--Littlewood comparisons.
